year.label: 1993 Alfa Romeo 155 V6 TI (DTM Class 1, Alfa Corse)

identity.real_world_identity_notes: The telemetry name "Alfa Romeo 155 TI V6" and internal id ks_alfa_romeo_155_v6 map to Alfa Romeo's factory Class 1 DTM touring car, fielded by the works Alfa Corse team from the 1993 season opener at Zolder and driven that year by Nicola Larini (1993 DTM champion) and Alessandro Nannini. Kunos Simulazioni's own product description for the DLC that ships this car names it "Alfa Romeo 155 Ti V6 '93", anchoring the content to the 1993 season rather than the 1994-1996 seasons in which the same nameplate also raced. The car is a tube-frame, four-wheel-drive Group A/Class 1 racer built around a production-derived monocoque; it shares only its exterior silhouette with the road-going 155 saloon and has no relation to the later Alfa Romeo 156 Superturismo already curated in this database (alfa-romeo-156-super-touring). Reviewed sources agree closely on the car's identity and season but do not agree on its transmission actuation: one detailed account states the 1993 car began the season with a traditional H-gate lever and only evolved to a sequential unit during that same season, while general profile pieces describe the car's transmission in loose, undated terms as a "sequential semi-automatic gearbox". A later (1996-season, chassis #005) example of the same nameplate is independently documented as using a "6-speed semi-sequential transaxle", consistent with the sequential unit being a later-in-life characteristic rather than the season-opening specification. No source reviewed here pins down which exact point in the 1993 season Kunos modeled, so the transmission actuation and internal construction are left conflicting/not-established rather than guessed.

Assetto Corsa 14923034 behavior and cockpit values were directly observed and are preserved as simulator overrides where the real baseline is unknown.

The standing-start clutch is derived from the mechanism this record already establishes, not observed. An H-pattern gate is a driver-shifted gearbox, and a driver-shifted gearbox has to be declutched to pull away from rest, whatever its construction. All five registered H-pattern archetypes carry `standing_start_clutch: required`, and of the 96 curated H-pattern records the 87 that establish the field all say required with no dissenting value. Unlike the blip derivations this one does not rest on gearbox construction, so an unknown `gearbox_type` does not block it. The guided drive is not cited for it: a drive establishes what the simulator demands, not what the real car needed.

Kunos Simulazioni's own Steam store description, the community Assetto Corsa database, and multiple independent motorsport-history sources all converge on the same identity: the 1993-season Alfa Romeo 155 V6 TI, an Alfa Corse works Class 1 DTM car driven by Nicola Larini and Alessandro Nannini. No existing curated record in this repository covers this car, so record_action is create-new.

No existing curated record in this repository covers this car, so record_action is create-new.

Every reviewed source that mentions gear count independently states six forward gears, with no conflicting figure found; no manufacturer-grade primary document was available to raise this above medium confidence. The 2010 photograph captioned as the 1993 Larini/Alfa Corse car shows a continuous, round, suede-wrapped MOMO rim with no fixed grip humps or flattened section. An independently photographed 1996-season example of the same nameplate shows the same round rim family, corroborating that this is the wheel style used on the model rather than a one-off fitment. The photograph shows the rim's upper section, marked with a yellow centering stripe, continuing unbroken around the top of the wheel rather than being cut away. Both reviewed cockpit photographs show the only instrumentation (an analog gauge, and a separate digital/switch panel in the later example) mounted on the dashboard rather than on the wheel itself; neither wheel carries an LCD, LED numeric readout, or other rim-integrated display. Neither reviewed cockpit photograph shows any LED or lamp array mounted on the wheel rim itself; any warning lamps visible are on the dashboard/switch panel. The reviewed sources did not establish the remaining technique and wheel fields, which stay unknown in the real-car baseline: /authentic_controls/transmission/gearbox_type, /authentic_controls/transmission/shift_pattern, /authentic_controls/transmission/standing_start_clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/throttle_lift, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/manual_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/throttle_lift, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/manual_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_blip.
